gordon:asplos:2002: Beyond the thesis, external reception runs largely through StreamIt itself: groups retargeting the language treat this paper's partitioning, layout, and communication scheduling as the reference compilation path. Huynh and colleagues mapped streaming applications onto multi-GPU systems, Wang and O'Boyle partitioned stream graphs with machine learning, and StreamX10 carried the approach to X10, while throughput-driven synthesis for pipelined multicores measured against it. The larger citation mass is more distant: the paper appears in many works as the example of compiling a stream language onto communication-exposed hardware, and a steady share cites its Raw results as evidence of what static orchestration can achieve. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure lives on in the bthies/streamit repository.
bruening:cgo:2003:
Beyond that lineage, the deepest external engagement comes from people who ran the system rather than merely cited it. Tool-building citations range across security, performance analysis, and software maintenance: Ruwase and Lam built their practical dynamic buffer overflow detector on DynamoRIO; helper-threaded prefetching on the Sun UltraSPARC CMP, online impact analysis via dynamic compilation, studies of bounded code caches, live detection and repair of false sharing, and software wear management for persistent memories all used it as their instrumentation substrate; and JIT instrumentation carried its approach into operating-system kernels. The users span the paper's own decade through to memory-access-pattern classification work at ASPLOS years later.

The larger mass of citations is thinner. In surveys and related-work sections DynamoRIO serves as a customary example of dynamic binary translation, named alongside other frameworks rather than engaged in detail, and a further group measures new systems against it or positions instrumentation designs relative to it. The record thus has two layers: a broad backdrop of brief mentions, and a steady core of substantive users for whom the infrastructure promise of the title was kept. The system lives on as an open-source project at DynamoRIO/dynamorio.
stephenson:pldi:2000: The analysis found its main audience in hardware compilation. High-level synthesis took up bitwidth inference as a recurring concern: Cong's group built bitwidth-aware scheduling and binding on the idea, and later work on range and bitmask analysis for hardware optimization extends the technique directly. BitValue inference, developed independently at about the same time, is a companion work cited alongside it, and the wordlength-allocation line of Constantinides, Cheung, and Luk treats the paper as a point of comparison. The benchmarks traveled as well — bitwidth-aware global register allocation reuses them — and a long tail of citations invokes the reported area, clock, and power gains as evidence that narrow-width computation is worth exploiting.
perkins:sosp:2009:
The reception runs through the automatic program repair literature that formed in the years after publication. GenProg took up the idea of automatically generating and validating patches, and Le Goues and colleagues' systematic study of automated repair measured its methods against ClearView's results; a steady stream of later repair papers position their techniques relative to it, and surveys of the field include it as a demonstration that deployed binaries can be patched without source code or human intervention.

Direct extensions are fewer but concrete: Schulte, DiLorenzo, and Weimer extended automated repair to binary and assembly programs on embedded devices, Long and Rinard's SPR staged its patch generation around ClearView's model, and Azim, Neamtiu, and Marvel carried automated patching to smartphone software. Beyond this engaged center, the bulk of the citing record is peripheral — ClearView appears in lists of repair and self-healing systems, or as evidence that runtime patching of deployed software is feasible — the pattern of a paper cited less for its machinery than for the possibility it demonstrated.
taylor:isca:2004: Beyond the project the evaluation is read in two registers. A band of core citations comes from groups that used the chip as an experimental substrate: thermal modeling and management of on-chip networks, gigabit routing on the software-exposed tiled microprocessor, a reconfigurable architecture for load-balanced rendering, software-based instruction caching for embedded processors, and the conservation cores work. A larger mass cites the measurements as evidence, drawing on the Pentium-III comparisons and stream results in arguments about tiled architectures. Most citations are peripheral, placing Raw in lists of tiled and multicore designs, and a portion of the influence is routed through successor tiled processors rather than the paper itself.
thies:micro:2007: In the citing literature the paper travels mostly as a passing reference: much of its record is unjudged, and among the judged citations the majority name it in a sentence in related-work discussions of pipeline parallelism, often in architecture papers some distance from its topic. A small engaged band did more. Komoda, Miwa, and Nakamura adopted the communication-overlap idea for OpenCL applications, JFlow reused its case studies to evaluate refactorings for flow-based parallelism, Fussli measured against it as a baseline, and a cache-based scheme for speculative parallelization adopted one of its ideas. The reception is that of a practical technique noted often and taken up occasionally. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure that underlies the work lives on in the bthies/streamit repository.
wilson:sigplan:1994:
The same relationship extended well beyond the group. In the judged external record the dominant citation act is use: the citing papers report research carried out inside SUIF, and an unusual share of them are core engagements rather than passing mentions. Wilson and Lam's context-sensitive pointer analysis for C was built in the infrastructure, as were Ghosh, Martonosi, and Malik's cache miss equations and their extension to caches of arbitrary associativity, Rivera and Tseng's data transformations for eliminating conflict misses, Beyls and D'Hollander's reuse-distance work, and Tseng's elimination of barrier synchronization.

The platform also crossed subfields. SUIF Explorer built directly on it; Liao, Devadas, and Keutzer used it for storage assignment to decrease code size; PICO-NPA used it in high-level synthesis of nonprogrammable hardware accelerators; the Zephyr abstract-syntax work took it as a subject of study. A thinner band of citations simply names SUIF as the example of a shared research compiler. On the whole the paper is cited less for its claims than for the system it distributes — reception in the form of work done with the tool.
ansel:pact:2014:
Outside the group the framework found the use it was designed for: research systems across several domains embed it as their search engine. PolyMage tunes its image-pipeline schedules with it; the Lift stencil-code generator and the verified-lifting work of Kamil and colleagues drive their searches through it; ApproxHPVM and ApproxTuner use it to navigate accuracy-performance tradeoffs; and FPGA-oriented projects, from Cong's composable accelerator generation to LAMDA, either run it directly or extend its technique ensemble. Uses stretch as far as tuning JPEG quantization for classification networks and Singh and Solar-Lezama's generation of formula simplifiers.

A comparable share of the citing literature meets the paper from the other side, as a measuring stick: new autotuners evaluate themselves against its bandit ensemble or position their designs relative to it. Beyond these engaged citations lies a broad peripheral mass that names OpenTuner as the standard example of a general-purpose autotuning framework, a sign that the name settled into the field's shared vocabulary. The framework lives on in the jansel/opentuner repository.
amarasinghe:pldi:1993: In the citing literature the paper serves chiefly as a fixed point of the distributed-memory compilation era: work on message-passing code generation positions its methods against the value-centric, polyhedral formulation, and much of the remaining record is brief. The sustained line of building is Ferner's, whose Paraguin compiler generated message-passing code using SUIF, whose later work revisited communication code generation algorithms for message-passing systems, and whose work on suppressing independent loops in packing nests extends the machinery directly. The decomposition literature, from Anderson's automatic computation and data decomposition to the Rice dHPF overpartitioning work and the EPPP compiler, took up its representations, and DISTAL carries the same concerns into distributed tensor algebra.
gordon:asplos:2006:
Beyond those descendants, the citing literature engaged the paper across a wide range, though much of it at a distance: multicore-compilation and parallel-language works cite its finding — that applications differ in their dominant form of parallelism and that a compiler can exploit all three forms together — as evidence, position their own mappers against its approach, or place it in surveys and lists of stream-compilation work. A substantial engaged band works with it concretely.

The most direct successors treat it as the baseline for stream partitioning: Wang and O'Boyle's work on partitioning streaming parallelism for multicores and their later machine-learning partitioner both measure against its heuristics. Its StreamIt benchmarks travel further, into studies of mapping stream programs onto heterogeneous multiprocessor systems and an evaluation of dynamic voltage and frequency scaling for stream programs, while Liquid Metal and adaptive input-aware compilation for graphics engines build directly with the compiler, and compiler techniques for massively scalable implicit task parallelism carry its ideas into task-parallel settings. The compiler and its benchmarks live on in the StreamIt infrastructure repository at bthies/streamit.
Ragan-Kelley:2017:HDA:3176926.3150211: Later work reaches this article as the accessible citation for Halide, and the judged record divides between a minority that engages the system or its central idea and a larger share that names Halide among schedule-based compilers and domain-specific languages. The engaged citations run the compiler — the synthetic depth-of-field pipeline for single-camera mobile phones among them — or carry the algorithm-schedule separation elsewhere: HeteroCL to software-defined reconfigurable computing, DISTAL and SWIRL to tensor-algebra and neural-network compilation, Exocompilation to hardware accelerators, automatic dataflow-graph partitioning to distributed deep learning. A portion of the citations reaches the paper through such successors, so part of its influence is routed through the lineage the idea created. The compiler lives on at halide/Halide.
solar-lezama:pldi:2005: In the wider literature the paper stands as the origin of sketching, and most substantive citations engage the idea rather than the StreamBit implementation. The generalization came quickly: Combinatorial sketching for finite programs carried the approach beyond bit-streaming and became the main reference for the Sketch line. The idea was adopted elsewhere — for synthesizing probabilistic programs, for synthesizing machine code from semantics, and for automated feedback generation for introductory programming assignments — while SMT-based optimization of embedded arithmetic measured against it. The larger mass of citations is list membership, crediting the paper in a sentence as the point where sketch-based synthesis began.
hall:computer:1996:
In the citing literature the article serves as the standard reference for SUIF, and the largest single share of judged citations comes from work that used the compiler rather than merely naming it. SUIF Explorer grew an interactive, interprocedural parallelizer out of the same analyses; the work on superword-level parallelism in the presence of control flow built on the infrastructure; compiler frameworks for speculative multithreading, instruction generators for hybrid reconfigurable systems, and the Pace toolset for performance prediction took SUIF as their platform; and the machine-learning compilation line that begins with using machine learning to focus iterative optimization ran its studies through it.

A smaller body cites the results as evidence rather than infrastructure, invoking the NAS and SPECfp95 measurements as the mark of what interprocedural automatic parallelization achieves on shared-memory machines. The rest of the record is broad and shallow: the article named in lists of parallelizing compilers across architecture, language, and embedded-systems venues. That profile — a core of users inside a much larger ring of listings — is the reception of an infrastructure paper, cited by a community for the system it was running.
olszewski:asplos:2009:
Beyond the project, deterministic multithreading grew into a research area, and the citing literature treats Kendo as one of its reference points. Most citations position new determinism systems against it or list it among the software-only approaches, but a core engaged closely: RCDC builds on it directly, Dthreads measures itself against it, and work on deterministic multithreading without global barriers and on memory-isolated determinism (esDMT) takes up its scheduling ideas. Its deterministic logical time, built from hardware performance counters, is the element most often carried forward.

The idea also traveled outside the determinism literature. Bunshin applies it to compositing security mechanisms through diversification, Memoir draws on it for state continuity in protected modules, work on detecting covert timing channels adopts it for time-deterministic replay, and FiberSCIP carries it into parallel mathematical optimization; real-time work uses Kendo as a baseline for worst-case execution-time calculation on multicores. The long tail of the record is peripheral — Kendo named in a sentence about determinism — but the engaged citations span systems, security, debugging, and solvers.
tiramisu: That turn toward learned optimization shaped the reception. The deepest external engagement uses Tiramisu as a research vehicle for machine-learning-driven compilation: Pearl's deep-reinforcement-learning optimizer, an experimental study of LLM-guided loop optimization, pre-trained performance models, the LOOPerSet dataset, and CHEHAB RL for homomorphic encryption all run on the compiler, and its affine machinery was carried into quantum circuit mapping; further afield, the CoRa tensor compiler used it in its work on ragged tensors. The much larger share of citations is list membership: across the tensor-compiler and scheduling-language literature, Tiramisu appears alongside other polyhedral and scheduling-language systems as a point on the map rather than a system engaged in detail.
ragankelley:halide:2012: In the citing record the paper serves as the gateway to the language itself: much of its reception comes from work that programs in Halide rather than merely discussing it. Camera pipelines including burst photography for high dynamic range imaging on mobile cameras and Fast Fourier Color Constancy were written in the language; Mullapudi and colleagues automated Halide scheduling; later work made Halide pipelines differentiable, translated existing image processing libraries into Halide, and retargeted the compiler to heterogeneous hardware and FPGAs through systems such as HeteroHalide. Around these users sits a broad periphery that cites the paper as the representative image-processing DSL when framing new compilers and languages. The compiler and its community live on at halide/Halide.
waingold:computer:1997:
The citing literature receives the article mostly as shorthand for a category of machines. Raw appears in surveys of on-chip parallelism and in the lists with which later architecture papers situate themselves, cited as the tiled design that hands wires, scheduling, and routing to the compiler; only a minority of the citations engage its mechanisms in detail. Papers proposing new architectures differentiate their choices from Raw's, and others draw on its arguments and measurements as evidence in debates over scaling and wire delay.

The deepest engagement stays close to the machine itself. Theses and companion papers within the project — software-based instruction caching, the SIFt streaming compiler, compilation to the exposed memory hierarchy, a Raw network router, and compiler support for scalable memory systems — treat the article as the definition of the platform they build on, and later Raw publications such as Versatile Tiled-Processor Architectures carry its description forward. Outside that circle the paper serves as a fixed point of reference: the design against which other tiled and configurable proposals explain themselves.
kiriansky-micro18-dawg:
In the citing literature DAWG stands as a fixed point in the design space of cache defenses. Much of the record is positional: papers proposing mitigations for speculative-execution and cache side-channel attacks place DAWG among the partitioning defenses and differentiate their designs from it, often by offering finer-grained or more scalable partitioning. Bespoke Cache Enclaves and Chunked-Cache measure against it as a baseline, as do speculation-focused defenses such as SpecShield and Speculative Privacy Tracking, and surveys of microarchitectural security put it in the partitioning branch of their taxonomies.

A smaller thread engages the security argument rather than the mechanism. Formal-methods work on modelling and verifying security-oriented resource partitioning takes DAWG as a subject, RTL2μPATH carries related questions into hardware security verification, attack-side works such as MicroScope and Safecracker pick up its ideas, and IVcache builds its evaluation directly against it. The great majority of citations, though, are brief: DAWG is a defense a paper in this area is expected to name, and most do so in a sentence or a table row.
lee:asplos:1998: The compiler carried much of the paper's reception: energy and power studies of tiled architectures and on-chip networks — the ISLPED energy characterization of a tiled processor, software-directed power-aware interconnection networks, high-level power analysis for on-chip networks — ran RAWCC in their experimental flows, and Swenson extended the spatial instruction scheduling directly. Within the project, Barua's compiler-managed memory line and Babb's compilation for gate-reconfigurable architectures grew out of the same machinery. Most other citations are briefer, naming the paper when introducing spatial compilation for distributed-resource machines, and part of its influence travels under the names of the later Raw papers rather than under its own.
kiriansky:security:2002: In the wider literature the paper serves as a common point of reference for execution monitoring: later defenses position their mechanisms against shepherding's policies, surveys of software security carry it forward, and a long tail cites it briefly among prior work. The closer engagements run through the infrastructure as much as the idea. Systems such as comprehensive kernel instrumentation via dynamic binary translation, PiPA, BlackBox, and work on binary compatibility for SGX enclaves build on the shepherding implementation and its DynamoRIO descendants, while a few works — securing the kernel via static binary rewriting and program shepherding, and the LAIDS/LIDS framework for systematic IPS design — take up the idea itself.
stephenson:pldi:2003: Beyond the thesis, the citing literature treats the paper as a reference point for machine-learned compiler heuristics. The most substantive engagement adopts the idea rather than the code: priority-function learning reappears in atomic block formation for explicit data graph execution architectures, in metaoptimization of inlining priority functions for TRIPS, in Cavazos and Moss's induced scheduling heuristics, and in machine-learning approaches to partitioning streaming parallelism for multi-cores. A larger mass of surveys and related-work sections cites the paper as an early demonstration of machine learning for compilers, and autotuning work differentiates its search strategies from the paper's genetic programming. Most citations are brief, but the substantive ones transplant the priority-function idea to new heuristics.
larsen:pldi:2000:
Beyond the group's own successors, the citing literature made superword-level parallelism a research area in its own right. One line reworks the packing algorithm itself: PSLP, VW-SLP, and SuperGraph-SLP restructure how statements are grouped and searched, while the SIMD defragmenter and a compiler framework for extracting superword-level parallelism measure their techniques against the original scheme. Another line, running through Superword-Level Parallelism in the Presence of Control Flow and Exploiting Superword-Level Locality in Multimedia Extension Architectures, carried the approach to branching code and to the memory hierarchy, and the compiler found an early user in the DIVA processing-in-memory chip project.

Around that core sits a much larger body of citation that treats SLP as shared vocabulary: papers on automatic vectorization position their techniques against it, cite its measurements as evidence for the value of parallelism inside basic blocks, or list it among the standard approaches alongside loop vectorization. Most of these engagements are brief, but the substantive minority — the works extending, adopting, or benchmarking against the algorithm — is large enough to form a distinct SLP vectorization literature, with this paper at its root.
kjolstad:oopsla:2017:
Beyond the project, the citing literature divides into a broad periphery and a working core. The periphery names taco in a sentence as the compiler approach to sparse tensor algebra; the core builds on it. DISTAL and SpDISTAL extend the compiler to distributed tensor algebra, Mosaic extends it to interoperate with external kernels, and SparseLNR and the compilation of modular and general sparse workspaces carry its code generation further. Other systems use it as infrastructure: BaCO autotunes against it, and architecture-side work such as The Sparse Abstract Machine and Phloem builds hardware compilation paths with it.

The compiler also serves as the field's measuring stick. Accelerator papers beginning with ExTensor take its generated kernels as the software baseline, formal work such as Indexed Streams takes its fused loops as the object to reason about, and dozens of evaluations reuse its workloads or position new sparse compilers relative to it. Taken together, the record shows a system run and extended by a core of follow-on projects, surrounded by a large literature for which taco is the default point of reference in sparse tensor compilation. The implementation lives in the tensor-compiler/taco repository, and the paper carries artifacts-available and artifacts-evaluated badges.
ansel:pldi:2009:
Beyond the project, the reception is broad but mostly at arm's length: to the citing literature PetaBricks is the name for algorithmic choice, and the bulk of the record cites it as the representative of that idea, in related-work lists, in surveys of autotuning and adaptive software, and as the design point against which new systems are positioned. A smaller band engaged directly. Elastic computing adopted the multiple-implementation premise, variant-based competitive parallel execution raced alternative variants of sequential programs, and HPAC drew on the approach for approximate computing in HPC OpenMP applications; a handful of works ran the compiler and autotuner themselves, among them parallel iterative compilation and a student reimplementation of PetaBricks in Julia.

The pattern is that of a reference point rather than a substrate: few external systems build on the implementation, but the vocabulary the paper introduced — poly-algorithms assembled from alternative rules and tuned alongside parameters — recurs wherever an autotuner's search space includes the algorithm itself, and part of the influence traveled onward through the project's own successors, OpenTuner among them. The compiler and autotuner live on at petabricks/petabricks.
ansel:ipdps:2009: The citation record bears that out: a large share of citing works run DMTCP rather than merely discuss it, and the tool turns up far from its original cluster targets — SweeD checkpoints likelihood computations over thousands of genomes, CRUM carries checkpoint-restart to CUDA's unified memory, and Kubernetes systems lean on it for stateful fault tolerance and seamless pod migration. Successor systems extend it directly, among them URDB and MANA for MPI, while transparent checkpoint-restart over InfiniBand and checkpointing as a service in heterogeneous clouds build on the same base. The rest of the citations place DMTCP in the standard roster of transparent checkpointing packages. The tool lives on as open-source software at dmtcp/dmtcp.
